title: Open sourced my multi-LLM trading platform which i've been using the past year.
author: ouwenbelg
selftext:
I run [https://quorumtrading.com](https://quorumtrading.com) and recently [open sourced it](https://github.com/COLARDYNIT/quorumtrading), wanted to know what you guys think.

The idea: instead of one model saying "buy", multiple AI agents debate every decision. A technical agent, a fundamental agent and a sentiment agent each read your strategy (plain markdown), look at the market data, and vote. No consensus, no trade. You can also let an orchestrator model overrule the vote, if you enjoy giving one LLM the final word. Quorum is the minumum amount of ppl who need to agree to make a decision, hence the name QuorumTrading. Heads up: there is already a shameless clone who almost copied the product word by word. I guess it's a compliment.

The workflow is deliberately boring: backtest against history first, paper trade second, real money only when the numbers stop embarrassing you. Backtesting is the core of the product, not an afterthought, because LLM agents are sometimes confidently wrong and no prompt fixes that. I loved using expensive models (opus, fable) to train dumb, dirt free models to make the correct decision at the correct time. It was a challange to create strategies which beat buy & hold of the best performing ETF's, but it's certainly possible.

Why open source: if you're going to let LLM handle your money, you'd want to know it's not vibecoded or at least has a decent architecture. Feel free to scrutenize the code, or self host it.

Works with stocks and crypto, bring your own model (API key or fully local). Hosted version is free to start (pay only for AI usage), self-hosting is free forever, no markup on model costs. AGPL-3.0.

Not financial advice, and the tool will happily lose money executing a bad strategy well. I've been running it on my own strategies since November. Feedback welcome!

comments.author: Interesting_Gold_792
comments.body:
Really interesting architecture. I’ve been experimenting with a different version of the same general problem: separating market evidence from the final decision instead of letting one model own the entire trade thesis.  
One thing I’m curious about with the quorum approach: have you tested situations where all three agents become correlated and confidently wrong together?  
For example, technical + sentiment + fundamental could all vote BUY, but execution conditions, liquidity or a regime change might still make the trade objectively bad.  
Have you experimented with deterministic veto gates outside the LLM council — things like liquidity, stale data, max risk, execution quality or regime uncertainty — that the orchestrator cannot override?  
I’d also be really interested in whether you’ve measured disagreement itself as useful information rather than just something preventing consensus.

replies.author: ouwenbelg
replies.body:
There are deterministic gates, but only for position size, reserve cash, buy order size etc. Nothing regarding liquidity or regime change. Might be interesting to add! But i also fear feature creap, and building a huge and complicated platform nobody wants to use nor maintain. Seen it happening too many times.

Multiple agents being confidently wrong together barely ever happens, but all depends on the LLMs used, and how hard the instructions are. Many technical indicators (sma, ema, rsi, macd, bollinger bands) are precalculated and handed over to the LLMs, so the models dont have to do math, but if you have complex instructions and choose the smallest models... your mileage may vary. Fun to find the sweetspot though!

replies.author: Interesting_Gold_792
replies.body:
That makes sense, especially the feature-creep concern. I like the separation of deterministic calculations from the LLM reasoning too — calculate the indicators once and let the agents interpret the evidence rather than asking them to do the math.  
I wonder if liquidity/regime doesn’t necessarily need to become another agent or large feature though. It could just be a very small deterministic veto layer before execution: if liquidity, spread, data freshness, or regime uncertainty crosses a hard threshold, no agent or orchestrator can override it.  
One thing I’m curious about: when the agents disagree, do you persist that disagreement anywhere? I wonder if the disagreement itself could become useful forward data — for example, whether high disagreement correlates with worse expectancy or regime transitions over time.

replies.author: ouwenbelg
replies.body: Yes, all reasoning is stored, so you can learn from the mistakes made by the agents. Also available via mcp tooling, so using claude code i often use opus/fable llm to ask "check the reasoning of the agents, did they make mistakes, and if so adapt the strategy and run a new backtest".

replies.author: Interesting_Gold_792
replies.body:
That’s really interesting. Persisting the reasoning makes the system much more useful than just storing the final vote.  
The part I’d be careful with is automatically adapting the strategy after reviewing mistakes, because it seems easy to accidentally optimize for the trades that just happened.  
Do you treat the adapted strategy as a completely new candidate and require it to beat the previous version on unseen/walk-forward data before promotion? Or can the review loop modify the active strategy directly?  
I’m curious how you’re preventing that reasoning → adaptation → backtest loop from gradually overfitting itself.

replies.author: ouwenbelg
replies.body:
Good questions, the same I had while developing it. :D Initially I had a self improving loop in the system itself, but that was replaced in favor of transparency what happened during the trading decisions. So now I just hook up claude code and tell opus/fable to run a backtest simulation using certain models and strategies, and see where it can improve the decisions made by the agents, without using the knowledge how the crypto/stock evaluated over time.

An EMA based strategy was the best working one, which beats the market even over 25y buy and hold: [https://quorumtrading.com/strategies/public/e9bf6663-2470-47ba-b639-07d62dd08ff9](https://quorumtrading.com/strategies/public/e9bf6663-2470-47ba-b639-07d62dd08ff9)

comments.author: invest0rZ
comments.body: Why would you give something like this away?

replies.author: ouwenbelg
replies.body: To increase trust in the product, and show its not a vibe coded mess.

replies.author: ouwenbelg
replies.body: Deepseek v4 flash works extremely well to create strategies, maybe a bit overkill to actually trade.

replies.author: invest0rZ
replies.body: What would you use to make the trades?

replies.author: ouwenbelg
replies.body: Gemini flash, deepseek and mistral where the cheapest which did not make mistakes following clear instructions. You can configure a different model per strategy, so I suggest to try multiple models and pick the cheapest one following your instructions without mistakes.
